body:
Why the Non-Aligned Movement emerged

After the Second World War, many Asian and African countries became independent from colonial rule. Although they had achieved political independence, they continued to face economic difficulties and pressure from the Cold War superpowers.

These countries sought a way to participate in international affairs without permanently associating themselves with either rival military bloc.

The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) emerged from this shared desire for political independence, peaceful cooperation and development.

The Bandung Conference, 1955

The Asian-African Conference was held at Bandung, Indonesia, from 18 to 24 April 1955.

Delegations representing 29 governments participated. The conference addressed colonialism, racial discrimination, economic development and peaceful international relations.

Bandung encouraged cooperation among Asian and African countries and helped create the political foundations of NAM.

However, the Bandung Conference was not the first official NAM summit. NAM was formally established later.

The founding leaders of NAM

Five leaders are particularly associated with the establishment of NAM.

LeaderCountryPrincipal contribution
Jawaharlal NehruIndiaAdvocated non-alignment and peaceful coexistence.
Josip Broz TitoYugoslaviaSupported independence from rival bloc domination.
Gamal Abdel NasserEgyptPromoted Arab nationalism and anti-colonialism.
SukarnoIndonesiaHosted the Bandung Conference.
Kwame NkrumahGhanaSupported African independence and unity.

Cooperation among these leaders helped turn non-alignment from a foreign-policy approach followed by individual countries into a broader international movement.

The first NAM summit, 1961

The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement took place in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, from 1 to 6 September 1961.

It brought together 25 countries.

This gathering marked the formal establishment of NAM as an international movement.

Major objectives of NAM

The movement encouraged its members to:

  • Protect national sovereignty and political independence.
  • Oppose colonialism, imperialism and racial discrimination.
  • Avoid involvement in rival superpower-led military blocs.
  • Promote peaceful settlement of international disputes.
  • Support economic development and cooperation among developing countries.
  • Seek a more representative international political and economic order.

Imperialism refers to the extension of a country's power or control over other territories or peoples. Decolonisation refers to the ending of colonial rule and the achievement of independence.

India's role in NAM

India was a founding member and an important advocate of NAM. Nehru promoted cooperation among newly independent states and supported Asian and African liberation movements.

India had already convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in March 1947, before independence. It also supported Indonesia's struggle against Dutch colonial rule.

Within NAM, India sought to preserve national independence while working with other developing countries on international issues.

From political independence to economic development

Members of NAM increasingly recognised that political independence would remain limited if developing countries depended heavily on wealthy countries for trade, technology and finance.

This concern contributed to demands for a New International Economic Order (NIEO).

In 1972, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) issued a report proposing reforms intended to improve the position of developing countries in the international economy.

Important demands included better access to developed-country markets, greater control over natural resources, improved access to technology and stronger representation in international economic institutions.

Economic questions became increasingly important to NAM during the 1970s. The NIEO initiative subsequently lost momentum, particularly during the 1980s, because of opposition from developed countries and differences among developing countries.

Institutional character of NAM

NAM is an international political movement rather than a military alliance. Unlike the United Nations, it does not have a formal founding charter or a permanent secretariat. Its coordination is undertaken through its chairmanship and associated meetings.

Prelims focus

  • Bandung Conference: Indonesia, 18-24 April 1955; 29 participating governments.
  • First NAM summit: Belgrade, Yugoslavia, 1-6 September 1961.
  • Participants at the first NAM summit: 25 countries.
  • Five founding leaders: Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah.
  • NIEO refers to the proposed New International Economic Order.
  • Trap: Bandung in 1955 and the first NAM summit in 1961 were different events.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapter 1, The Cold War Era, printed pp. 10-13; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, printed p. 68; Non-Aligned Movement, History, official Uganda Chairmanship website, sections on Bandung and the First Summit, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The Bandung Conference brought Asian and African countries together to discuss independence, peace and development.

title: The Non-Aligned Movement: Origins, Founders and International Role

body:
Friendly relations after independence

India initially sought friendly relations with the People's Republic of China, which was established in 1949.

India was among the early countries to recognise the new Chinese government. Nehru believed that cooperation between India and China could strengthen Asian solidarity and reduce international tensions.

The adoption of Panchsheel in 1954 reflected this approach. However, differences over Tibet and the boundary between the 2 countries gradually weakened their relationship.

The Tibet question

Tibet occupies a strategically important region between India and China.

China established control over Tibet in 1950. India became increasingly concerned about developments there and the consequences for its northern security.

The Dalai Lama, Tibet's spiritual leader, entered India and was granted asylum in 1959 after unrest and Chinese military action in Tibet.

China strongly objected to the asylum and alleged that activities hostile to China were being conducted from Indian territory.

These developments increased diplomatic tensions between the 2 countries.

The territorial dispute

India and China also disagreed over the location of their boundary, particularly in 2 regions.

Aksai Chin

Aksai Chin lies in the western sector of the India-China boundary, in the Ladakh region. India claims Aksai Chin as part of its territory, while China controls the area.

During the late 1950s, China established a strategic road through the disputed area. This contributed to the deterioration of relations.

North-East Frontier Agency

The eastern dispute concerned territory then administered as the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), corresponding broadly to present-day Arunachal Pradesh.

China challenged the boundary accepted by India. Diplomatic discussions failed to resolve these differences.

The India-China War of 1962

In October 1962, Chinese forces launched major attacks in the western and eastern sectors of the disputed boundary.

The conflict occurred during the same month as the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the USA and USSR were involved in a major confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba.

Chinese forces made significant advances, particularly in the eastern sector. China announced a unilateral ceasefire in November 1962. Although fighting stopped, the territorial dispute remained unresolved.

Consequences for India

The war significantly affected India's foreign and security policies.

  • Security concerns: India recognised the need to improve military preparedness and strengthen border defence.
  • Defence modernisation: The government increased its attention to defence capabilities and military equipment.
  • International assistance: India sought military assistance from the USA and Britain during the conflict.
  • Domestic political consequences: Defence Minister V. K. Krishna Menon resigned during the war, and Nehru's government faced strong criticism.
  • Economic consequences: Greater defence expenditure placed additional pressure on resources needed for development.

The conflict demonstrated that peaceful coexistence and non-alignment could not substitute for adequate national defence.

Gradual restoration of relations

Relations remained strained for several years. Full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976.

In 1979, Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited China as India's External Affairs Minister. This was an important step in renewed diplomatic engagement.

These developments showed that countries could attempt to restore diplomatic relations even when territorial disagreements had not been fully resolved.

Prelims focus

  • The People's Republic of China was established in 1949.
  • China established control over Tibet in 1950.
  • The Dalai Lama received asylum in India in 1959.
  • The India-China War took place in 1962.
  • Important disputed regions included Aksai Chin and NEFA.
  • Full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976.
  • Trap: The 1962 ceasefire did not settle the territorial dispute.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, India's External Relations, printed pp. 68-73; Ministry of External Affairs, Panchsheel, June 2004, section on the 1954 India-China relationship, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline showing friendly India–China relations giving way to Tibet and boundary tensions, the 1962 war, and restored diplomatic relations in 1976.
pictures.caption: The deterioration in relations resulted from the combination of disagreements over Tibet and the boundary.

title: India-China Relations: Panchsheel, Tibet and the War of 1962

body:
Background: Partition and Kashmir

India and Pakistan became independent in August 1947. Partition was followed by population movements, communal violence and disputes concerning the accession of princely states.

Armed conflict developed over Jammu and Kashmir in 1947-1948. The dispute subsequently became a major source of tension between the 2 countries.

Nevertheless, India and Pakistan also cooperated on certain issues, including the Indus Waters Treaty signed in 1960. This demonstrates that political conflict did not prevent every form of diplomatic negotiation.

The India-Pakistan War of 1965

The 1965 conflict is particularly relevant to Gujarat because its early phase involved the Rann of Kutch.

Initial clashes in Gujarat

In April 1965, Pakistani forces launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat.

The Rann of Kutch is a salt-marsh region in western Gujarat adjoining Pakistan. Its border location made it strategically important.

Although fighting in the Rann of Kutch was limited compared with the subsequent war, it formed part of the deterioration of India-Pakistan relations in 1965.

Escalation in Jammu and Kashmir

During August and September 1965, Pakistan launched a larger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir.

The Indian government, led by Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri, responded militarily. Indian forces also launched a counter-offensive across the Punjab border to reduce pressure on the Kashmir front.

Fierce fighting followed. Indian troops advanced towards Lahore, while both countries suffered military and economic losses.

The Tashkent Declaration

Following a ceasefire and Soviet diplomatic mediation, India and Pakistan signed the Tashkent Declaration on 10 January 1966.

The declaration was signed by Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistani President Ayub Khan.

It provided for efforts to restore peaceful relations and for withdrawal of armed personnel to the positions held before 5 August 1965, by 25 February 1966.

The declaration did not permanently resolve the Kashmir dispute.

The Bangladesh Liberation War and India-Pakistan War of 1971

Background in East Pakistan

Before 1971, Pakistan consisted of geographically separated western and eastern parts. East Pakistan had a Bengali-speaking majority and faced longstanding political and economic grievances.

In Pakistan's general elections of 1970, the Awami League led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman secured an electoral majority. The Pakistani leadership did not transfer national power to the party.

In March 1971, the Pakistani military launched a crackdown in East Pakistan. Large numbers of people fled to India, creating a major refugee crisis.

India's involvement

India, led by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, provided political, humanitarian and other support to the Bangladesh liberation struggle.

The regional situation was complicated by the diplomatic relationship between Pakistan, the USA and China.

India signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with the USSR on 9 August 1971. It strengthened India's diplomatic position during the crisis.

War and the independence of Bangladesh

Full-scale war between India and Pakistan began in December 1971.

Indian armed forces operated on the eastern and western fronts. In the east, Indian forces advanced with support from Bangladeshi liberation forces.

On 16 December 1971, Pakistani forces surrendered in Dhaka. Bangladesh emerged as an independent country.

The war changed the political geography of South Asia. It also increased India's international standing while demonstrating the importance of military capability and diplomatic support.

Distinguishing the major conflicts

ConflictMain issuePrincipal outcome
1947-1948Jammu and KashmirCeasefire without final settlement of the dispute
1962India-China boundary disputeMajor defence reassessment in India
1965India-Pakistan conflict involving Gujarat, Kashmir and PunjabTashkent Declaration, 1966
1971Political crisis and liberation struggle in East PakistanIndependence of Bangladesh

Prelims focus

  • The Rann of Kutch clashes occurred in April 1965.
  • Lal Bahadur Shastri was India's Prime Minister during the 1965 war.
  • Tashkent Declaration: 10 January 1966.
  • Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister during the 1971 war.
  • India-USSR Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation: 9 August 1971.
  • Bangladesh Liberation War: 1971; surrender in Dhaka on 16 December 1971.
  • Trap: The 1965 war involved the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat; the 1971 war resulted in the independence of Bangladesh.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, India's External Relations, printed pp. 74-78; Ministry of External Affairs, Tashkent Declaration, 10 January 1966, clauses I-II; Ministry of External Affairs, Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation between India and the USSR, 9 August 1971; consulted 22 November 2026.]
